procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 01.04.2016 by the High Court of Himachal Pradesh, Shimla in Criminal Appeal No. 75 and 227 of 2015.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Sessions Judge (Forests), Shimla, dated 31st December, 2014 in Sessions Trial No.39-S/7 of 2012 convicted the appellant under Section 304 Part-II of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The High Court of Himachal Pradesh, Shimla in Criminal Appeal Nos.75 & 227 of 2015, modified the order of conviction and sentence passed by the Sessions Judge (Forests), Shimla, dated 31st December, 2014 in Sessions Trial No.39-S/7 of 2012 thereby convicting the appellant under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and sentencing him to imprisonment for life along with fine. The High Court affirmed the order of acquittal in favor of the other accused who were tried along with the appellant.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The original accused No.1 (Atul Thakur) appealed to the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's decision to convict him under Section 302 of the IPC instead of Section 304 Part-II.

decision.conviction_status: The appellant is held guilty for an offence punishable under Section 304 Part-II of IPC.
decision.sentence_status: sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of 10 (Ten) years with fine of Rs.10,000/- (Rupees Ten Thousand), in default to undergo further imprisonment for one year.
directions: The appellant shall be entitled to set off under Section 428 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

issue.issue_text: Whether the involvement of the appellant in the commission of the crime was proved beyond a reasonable doubt, thereby warranting an acquittal.

facts: The appellant argued that his involvement in the crime was not proven beyond a reasonable doubt and that he should be acquitted like his co-accused.
The prosecution presented evidence from two eyewitnesses (PW-11 and PW-12) who saw the appellant assault the deceased.
Other circumstantial evidence included the recovery of the knife at the appellant's instance and the nature of the injuries suffered by the deceased, which were attributable to that knife.
law: In criminal cases, the prosecution must prove the accused's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
An appellate court generally upholds concurrent findings of fact by lower courts unless there is a clear error.
application: The Supreme Court carefully considered the oral evidence from the eyewitnesses and the other circumstantial evidence.
The Court noted that both the Trial Court and the High Court had already analyzed this evidence and found it sufficient to prove the appellant's complicity in the crime.
The Supreme Court agreed with the 'concurrent finding' of the two lower courts, stating that they had justly analyzed the evidence.
Based on this evidence, the Court was satisfied that the appellant had caused the six knife injuries to the deceased, which resulted in his death.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that his involvement in the commission of the crime was established beyond a reasonable doubt. It therefore upheld the concurrent findings of the lower courts regarding his complicity and denied his plea for acquittal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the action of the accused which caused the death of the deceased would amount to murder under Section 302 of the IPC or culpable homicide not amounting to murder, falling under Exception 4 to Section 300 of the IPC.

facts.fact: The appellant and the deceased were friends with cordial relations, and the incident occurred at a drink party arranged by the deceased.
The assault was not premeditated. It happened suddenly during a quarrel that started when the deceased blew smoke in the appellant's face.
A sudden physical fight ensued, and in the "heat of passion," the appellant stabbed the deceased six times with a knife.

After the assault, the appellant's conduct showed a lack of intention to kill: he offered the deceased water, took him to the hospital, stayed with him until he died, and called the deceased's father.

law.law_name: Exception 4 to Section 300 of the IPC
law.description: This exception reduces the charge from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder if the act is committed without premeditation, in a sudden fight, in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and without the offender taking undue advantage or acting in a cruel or unusual manner.

The Court held that neither the use of a weapon like a knife nor the number of injuries inflicted are, by themselves, decisive factors to deny the benefit of Exception 4. The court must take an overall view of all the established facts and circumstances.

application.reasoning: The Court found that all the conditions of Exception 4 were met. The evidence clearly established there was no premeditation, and the assault occurred during a sudden fight that arose from a trivial quarrel in the heat of passion.

The appellant's actions after the incident (offering water, taking the deceased to the hospital) demonstrated that he had not taken undue advantage or acted in a cruel manner, and that he had no intention to cause death.

The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had made a "manifest error" by focusing too heavily on the use of a knife and the number of blows. It emphasized that these factors alone were not enough to classify the act as murder, especially when weighed against the other circumstances.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the appellant's action did not amount to murder under Section 302 of the IPC. Instead, it was a case of culpable homicide not amounting to murder, falling squarely within Exception 4 to Section 300 of the IPC. Consequently, the Court set aside the High Court's murder conviction and convicted the appellant under Section 304 Part-II of the IPC.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the involvement of the appellant in the commission of the crime was proved beyond a reasonable doubt, thereby warranting an acquittal.
appellant_arguments: There are obvious contradictions in the evidence of the eyewitnesses.
The genesis of the offence is doubtful.
The appellant's involvement in the crime has not been proved beyond a reasonable doubt.
The appellant deserves to be acquitted, similar to the co-accused.
respondent_arguments: The finding of guilt by the lower courts is supported by the evidence on record.
The evidence has established the appellant's involvement in the commission of the crime beyond any doubt.
The concurrent findings of guilt by the Trial Court and the High Court do not warrant interference.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the action of the accused which caused the death of the deceased would amount to murder under Section 302 of the IPC or culpable homicide not amounting to murder, falling under Exception 4 to Section 300 of the IPC.
appellant_arguments: The established facts do not warrant a conviction for murder under Section 302 IPC.
The case is one of culpable homicide not amounting to murder, covered by Exception 4 to Section 300 of the IPC.
The incident occurred without premeditation, during a sudden fight that arose in the heat of passion.
The appellant's actions after the assault, such as offering water and taking the deceased to the hospital, demonstrate a lack of intention to cause death.
The offence should be punishable under Section 304 Part-II of the IPC.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's conviction of the appellant under Section 302 IPC for murder is unexceptionable and just.
The use of a knife and the infliction of multiple (six) blows on the deceased indicate an intention to kill, constituting murder.

cases.case_name: Surain Singh v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: To restate the settled legal position regarding Exception 4 to Section 300 of the IPC, specifically that neither the use of a weapon nor the fact of multiple blows can be the sole basis to deny the benefit of this exception. The court must take an overall view of the matter, considering if the occurrence was sudden, not premeditated, and the offender acted in the heat of passion.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Neither the use of a weapon, such as a knife, nor the infliction of multiple blows can, by themselves, be the sole basis for denying an accused the benefit of Exception 4 to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code. The court must consider the overall context, including whether the act occurred without premeditation during a sudden fight and in the heat of passion, to determine if an offence is culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
obiter: When an assault resulting in death arises from a trivial reason, involves a weapon, and includes multiple blows, a light punishment is not warranted even if the conviction is for culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellant's act constitutes culpable homicide not amounting to murder, as the evidence establishes that the assault occurred without premeditation during a sudden fight that arose in the heat of passion. The appellant's post-assault conduct, such as offering water to the deceased and taking him to the hospital, further indicates a lack of intention to cause death. However, considering the trivial reason for the altercation, the use of a knife, and the infliction of multiple blows, a light punishment is not warranted, and a sentence of ten years imprisonment would meet the ends of justice.
legal_tests_applied: To determine if a case falls under Exception 4 to Section 300 of the IPC, the relevant factors are whether the occurrence was sudden and not premeditated, and if the offender acted in the heat of passion during a sudden fight without taking undue advantage or acting in a cruel manner.
The number of wounds caused by the appellant by itself cannot be a decisive factor to negate the application of Exception 4 to Section 300 of the IPC.

Neither the use of a weapon like a knife nor the factum of multiple injuries can be the sole basis to deny the benefit of Exception 4 to Section 300 of the IPC; the court is obliged to take an overall view of the matter based on established facts.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's plea for complete acquittal was rejected as the court upheld the concurrent findings of the Trial Court and High Court regarding his involvement in the commission of the crime.

The appellant's argument to restore the Trial Court's sentence of five years was rejected because the nature of the offense, the trivial reason for the assault, the use of a knife, and the infliction of multiple blows do not warrant a light punishment.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position that the appellant's involvement in the crime was proven beyond a doubt was accepted, as the court did not interfere with the concurrent findings of guilt recorded by the lower courts.

The respondent's argument for a substantial sentence was accepted, with the court holding that in the fact situation of the present case, the sentence period should not be less than 10 years imprisonment with fine to meet the ends of justice.
policy_considerations: The sentence must be proportionate to the crime to meet the ends of justice. Even when an act is not murder, a light punishment is not warranted when the assault, involving a knife and multiple blows, was triggered by a trivial reason, as this would not adequately reflect the gravity of the violence.
